I didn't eat half a loaf of bread in one sitting, but I know I could. And that is with the P, the B, and the J.

Over the last few years I've been cutting down carbs and I've learned something. Processed carbs are not filling. They might sate me for an while, but long before the next meal, I will be hungry again.

What I've realized is that there just isn't enough nutritional value in carb based foods to give my body what it needs. So no matter how much I eat, I still starving myself. And still I crave it, because that's the only food my body knows.

Since switching to higher meat & veg ration, my interest in carbs has gone way down. I didn't even enjoy spaghetti the last two times I've had it.

I'm healthier in another way now. I've learned that carbs make me constipated. It's not gluten not IBS, just straight up constipation. Even Rice and Potatoes. I don't know what it is that does it. The biggest surprise was processed meats: wieners, baloney, etc....

I was on antibiotics last week for an infection. Antibiotics can't discriminate between good bacteria and bad bacteria, so my gut flora got messed up. I've been constipated all this week and it reminded me what my life was like the last several years before I started cutting carbs.

Time to get back on the good diet. Time to stop letting what I eat slow me down.
I love me some PBnJ, but the fact that I can half a loaf of bread in one sitting can't be healthy.

I looking to get into shape (I'm one of those skinny girls who are ironically very unfit) and I want to start by running. Currently I can only run for about 3 minutes or so before being out of breath so I know it's going to be a slow start. Really I came here because I want any advice anyone here can give me. My big questions: how can I start (being how terrible I am), how can I stay motivated, how many days a week should I do it, what kind of running shoes are best, what stretches should I do beforehand, What kind is water bottle is best and lightweight, what kind of clothes should I wear, and should I start walking first before moving on to running. I should mention that there is a walkway near why house which is about 1 mile one way (so it'd be about 2.8 miles from my house and back total). Also, I'm thinking listening to music would keep me going longer so I want to get a small mp3, would an ipod shuffle be good for this?

Finally, I live in Canada. What should I do during the winter months? I'm thinking of joining a gym but is there any alternative to running that's not on a treadmill for those many, many cold months?

Any advice is appreciated! :)

If you want a small music player, there is no better option than a shuffle. But you can also get these armbands, where you can use your phone.

It is possible to run during winter, both inside and outside. Just wear the appropriate clothes, and as far as it isn't below -15C you should be good. There's also cross country skiing, spinning, elliptical machines, rowing machines, and much more.

For the winters, I'd say look for a community center/gym with an indoor track if you want to run but hate treadmills. Or you can take cardio classes, play recreational basketball/volleyball/badminton. It's certainly not the same as running outdoors but it could be a fun way to stay in decent shape during the bad months.

Lots of great, thorough advice, particularly from /u/KurayaminoKai and /u/misha_is_here. I would add that most people (myself included) start out running too fast. While speed work definitely has a place in training, I feel that when first starting out, building an aerobic base is the first hurdle and benefits more from duration than intensity.

There are some initial adaptations that are largely unrelated to the legs or the cardiovascular system but necessary for training. First, you just need the confidence to get out there and put some miles behind you, and easy effort builds confidence and increases compliance. Having an established program can help with this (mandatory C25k shot out). Secondly, you need to learn fundamental biofeedback. That is, you need to learn how to gauge your effort, and in doing so, how to push yourself without exhausting yourself prematurely or, worse, injuring yourself. Lastly, it may be a bit pseudo-science-y, but your body may need to "learn" how to sweat. If you don't regularly exert yourself in a warm environment, your body is less accustomed to sweating and will require higher body temperature to initiate the cooling procedure. This will make beginning running less comfortable and even a bit dangerous. Drink more water, and use a gentle beginning as an excuse to be outdoors as much as anything else.

Just because I saw no one mention it (perhaps because it's obvious), you can take a break from running in the winter and supplant it with something else. You would have to adjust back to running in the spring, but if you're active during the winter with skiing, skating, indoor exercise, etc. the transition will be easier than when starting out. Even just bundling up and trudging through snow for exercise would help retain some aerobic conditioning.

People telling you C25K are absolutely correct.
